desc: Spot the multiplier hidden in a short sequence.
hint: Compare each term to twice the previous term.
situation: Complete the series: 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, ?
title: Number series: doubling pattern
why: Each term is (2 × previous term) + 1: 3×2+1=7, 7×2+1=15, 15×2+1=31, 31×2+1=63. So the next term is 63×2+1 = 127.

desc: Find the constant interval between letters.
hint: Count positions in the alphabet: B=2, E=5, H=8…
situation: Complete the series: B, E, H, K, N, ?
title: Letter series: fixed step
why: B(2) → E(5) → H(8) → K(11) → N(14): each step adds 3. 14+3 = 17, and the 17th letter is Q.

desc: Look at the gaps between terms, not the terms themselves.
hint: Write down the differences between consecutive terms.
situation: Complete the series: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
title: Number series: rising differences
why: Differences: 6−2=4, 12−6=6, 20−12=8, 30−20=10 — rising by 2 each time. The next difference is 12, so the next term is 30+12 = 42.

choices: Every analyst on the audit team may enter the data hall.
Everyone who may enter the data hall is an analyst on the audit team.
No analyst on the audit team completed the security briefing.
Everyone with badge access completed the security briefing.
desc: Chain three universal statements without reversing any of them.
hint: Link them: analyst → briefing → badge → data hall. Then check which choice follows that exact direction.
situation: Premise 1: Every analyst on the audit team completed the security briefing. Premise 2: Everyone who completed the security briefing has badge access. Premise 3: Only people with badge access may enter the data hall. Which statement MUST be true?
title: Syllogism: three-premise chain
why: Chain the universals forward: analyst → completed the briefing (P1) → has badge access (P2) → may enter the data hall (P3, since badge access is the requirement). So every analyst may enter — choice 0. Choice 1 reverses the chain (affirming the consequent). Choice 2 directly contradicts Premise 1. Choice 3 reverses Premise 2 (completing the briefing is sufficient for badge access, not necessary).

choices: Every person who may approve equipment is a safety inspector.
Some safety inspectors may approve equipment.
No one outside the hazard course may approve equipment.
Everyone who may approve equipment has inspected safety.
desc: Chain two universal statements and check the overlap.
hint: Chain them: inspector → hazard course → may approve. Which choice says something weaker than 'all'?
situation: Premise 1: Every safety inspector has completed the hazard course. Premise 2: Everyone who has completed the hazard course may approve equipment. Which single statement MUST be true?
title: Syllogism: universal chains
why: Chaining: every inspector completed the course, and everyone who completed the course may approve equipment — therefore every inspector may approve equipment, so certainly some inspectors may approve: choice 1. Choice 0 reverses the chain (affirming the consequent). Choice 2 claims exclusivity the premises never state. Choice 3 invents 'has inspected safety', which appears nowhere.

desc: Every choice shares a property except one — find the break.
hint: All are perfect squares. Look at whether the roots are odd or even.
situation: Which number does NOT belong with the others?
title: Odd one out: squares of odd vs. even
why: All four are perfect squares: 121=11², 169=13², 225=15², 256=16². The roots 11, 13, 15 are all odd; only 256 is the square of an even number (16). So 256 is the odd one out.

desc: Place five people using positional clues.
evidence: Positions 1-2-3-4-5. Clue 1 → locked pair [Amal, Bex]. Clue 2 → locked pair [Cora, Dev]. Clue 3 → Eli at position 1. Two pair orders possible in positions 2-5: [A,B][C,D] or [C,D][A,B]. Clue 4: Amal left of Cora → only E A B C D works (E C D A B puts Amal at 4, Cora at 2). Unique solution: Eli, Amal, Bex, Cora, Dev. Position 3 = Bex.
hint: Treat 'Amal-Bex' and 'Cora-Dev' as two locked pairs, then test where Eli (the left end seat) forces the pairs to go.
situation: Five analysts — Amal, Bex, Cora, Dev, Eli — sit in a row of five chairs, left to right. Clues: (1) Bex sits immediately to the right of Amal. (2) Dev sits immediately to the right of Cora. (3) Eli sits in the leftmost chair. (4) Amal sits somewhere to the left of Cora. Who sits in the middle chair (position 3)?
title: Seating puzzle: five in a row
why: Clues 1 and 2 create two locked pairs: [Amal, Bex] and [Cora, Dev]. With Eli fixed at position 1, the pairs fill positions 2–5 in one of two orders: [Amal, Bex][Cora, Dev] or [Cora, Dev][Amal, Bex]. Clue 4 (Amal left of Cora) kills the second order (there Amal is right of Cora). Unique arrangement: Eli, Amal, Bex, Cora, Dev. Position 3 is Bex.

desc: Crack a simple A=1, B=2… word code and apply it.
hint: First confirm the rule with LAMP: L=12, A=1, M=13, P=16.
situation: In a certain code, each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet (A=1, B=2, …, Z=26), and a word's code is the SUM of its letters' values. LAMP codes to 42. What does DESK code to?
title: Letter-value code

desc: Successive percentage changes do not cancel — compute the net.
hint: Pick an easy original price, like $100, and track it through both changes.
situation: A laptop's price is raised by 25%, and later the new price is reduced by 20%. Compared with the original price, the final price is:
title: Percent up, then percent down
why: Start with $100. +25% → $125. −20% of $125 = $25 off → $100. The changes cancel exactly because 1.25 × 0.80 = 1.00, so the final price equals the original.

desc: Split a total according to a ratio, then adjust it.
hint: First find the current liters of each part. Adding solution doesn't change the water.
situation: A 60-liter tank holds cleaning solution and water in the ratio 2:3. How many liters of cleaning solution must be ADDED to make the ratio 3:2?
title: Ratio mixture
why: Ratio 2:3 over 60 L → solution = (2/5)×60 = 24 L, water = 36 L. Let x be liters added: (24+x)/36 = 3/2 → 2(24+x) = 108 → 48+2x = 108 → 2x = 60 → x = 30 liters.

desc: Work backward from an average to find a missing value.
hint: Total points before minus total points after equals the dropped score.
situation: The average of six test scores is 84. After the lowest score is dropped, the average of the remaining five scores is 87. What was the dropped score?
title: Average after removing a score
why: Total of six = 6×84 = 504. Total of five = 5×87 = 435. Dropped score = 504 − 435 = 69.

desc: Add rates, not times, when people work together.
hint: A's rate is 1/3 job per hour; B's is 1/6. Add them.
situation: Printer A can finish a job in 3 hours working alone; Printer B can finish the same job in 6 hours alone. Working together, how long to finish one job?
title: Combined work rate
why: Combined rate = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 job per hour. Time = 1 ÷ (1/2) = 2 hours.

desc: Pull the right two cells from a table and compute percent change.
hint: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old. The 'old' value is Q3.
situation: A regional office reports quarterly revenue (in thousands): Q1 2025: 410, Q2 2025: 445, Q3 2025: 380, Q4 2025: 470. What was the percent change from Q3 to Q4 2025?
title: Table reading: quarterly revenue change
why: Q3 = 380, Q4 = 470. Change = 470 − 380 = 90. Percent change = 90 ÷ 380 = 0.2368… ≈ +23.7%. (The 'thousands' units cancel — using 380 and 470 directly is fine.)

desc: Weight each group's average by its size.
hint: Total points = 12×78 + 8×93, divided by 20 people.
situation: A support team has 12 junior agents averaging 78 points and 8 senior agents averaging 93 points on a skills test. What is the team's overall average?
title: Weighted average: blended team score
why: Junior total = 12×78 = 936. Senior total = 8×93 = 744. Combined = 1680 points over 20 agents → 1680 ÷ 20 = 84.

desc: When two things move toward each other, their speeds add.
hint: Their closing speed is the sum of the two speeds.
situation: Two depots are 300 km apart. A van leaves Depot X heading toward Depot Y at 60 km/h; at the same moment a truck leaves Depot Y heading toward Depot X at 90 km/h. After how many hours do they meet?
title: Meeting point: two vehicles
why: Closing speed = 60 + 90 = 150 km/h. Time = distance ÷ speed = 300 ÷ 150 = 2 hours.

choices: A better deal for the customer
A worse deal for the customer
desc: Compare two 15% discounts in a row with one 30% discount.
hint: Try $100: after the first 15% it's $85 — now take 15% off $85.
situation: A store offers '15% off, then an additional 15% off the reduced price.' Compared with a single 30% discount on the original price, the two-step offer is:
title: Successive discounts vs. single discount
why: $100 → 15% off → $85 → another 15% off $85 = $12.75 off → $72.25. A single 30% off $100 = $70. The customer pays $72.25 vs $70, so the two-step offer is worse for the customer (0.85×0.85 = 0.7225, i.e. 27.75% off).

desc: Use the sentence's logic to pin down an unfamiliar word.
hint: The 'but' contrasts the conclusion with the 'thorough research' — yet the conclusion only *looks* fine.
situation: The committee praised the report's thorough research but rejected its specious conclusion. In this sentence, 'specious' most nearly means:
title: Vocabulary in context: 'specious'
why: 'Specious' means superficially plausible but actually wrong. The contrast structure ('praised…but rejected') tells you the conclusion seemed acceptable yet failed — exactly 'plausible but actually wrong.' 'Poorly researched' contradicts the praised research; 'highly detailed' and 'controversial' miss the deceptive-plausibility sense.

desc: Infer a word's meaning from how the sentence uses it.
hint: What behavior does the sentence illustrate? Checking everything twice, catching tiny errors.
situation: The scrupulous auditor checked every receipt twice and flagged even a two-cent discrepancy. Here, 'scrupulous' most nearly means:
title: Vocabulary in context: 'scrupulous'
why: The sentence shows painstaking thoroughness driven by integrity — 'meticulous and principled.' 'Suspicious' adds a motive the sentence doesn't state; 'slow and hesitant' confuses care with indecision; the last choice narrows the word to rule-following, missing the diligence sense.

desc: Let 'although' tell you the blank must reverse direction.
hint: 'Although' sets up a contrast: bad forecast vs. good weather. How would organizers feel?
situation: Although the forecast predicted heavy rain all weekend, the festival organizers were ______ when Saturday dawned clear and sunny.
title: Sentence completion: contrast signal
why: The contrast is forecast-bad vs. reality-good, so the reaction should be positive: 'relieved' fits. 'Dismayed' is negative (wrong direction), 'vindicated' would require them to have predicted the good weather themselves, and 'indifferent' ignores the stakes entirely.

desc: Both blanks must satisfy the sentence's logic at once.
hint: The result clause tells you what was missing: the team couldn't tell success from failure — the feedback lacked what quality?
situation: The manager's feedback was neither ______ nor ______, leaving the team unsure whether their work had succeeded or failed.
title: Sentence completion: double blank
why: The team is unsure about outcomes, so the feedback must have lacked clarity about what to do differently — 'specific' and 'actionable' both explain that gap. 'Harsh/encouraging' concerns tone, not informativeness; 'timely/relevant' and 'honest/direct' don't directly explain why success vs. failure was unknowable.

choices: Employees on floors 1–3 may use the north stairwell on Tuesday.
Equipment must be carried via the south stairwell.
Employees on floor 5 should avoid the north stairwell Monday–Wednesday.
The freight elevator is available to all employees this week.
desc: Draw only the conclusion the text actually supports.
hint: Eliminate any choice that adds facts the notice never states.
situation: Notice: 'The north stairwell will be closed for repairs Monday through Wednesday. Employees on floors 4–6 should use the south stairwell; the freight elevator remains available for equipment only.' Which statement is best supported?
title: Paragraph inference: office notice
why: Floor 5 is within 4–6, so those employees are told to use the south stairwell while the north is closed Mon–Wed — choice 2 restates that directly. Choice 0 assumes floors 1–3 can use a closed stairwell (the notice says it's closed, period). Choice 1 contradicts 'freight elevator…for equipment.' Choice 3 contradicts 'for equipment only.'

choices: No staff meetings can occur on the second floor on Thursdays in November.
Every staff member attends training every Thursday in November.
Some staff will be in second-floor meeting rooms on Thursdays in November.
Training sessions are the only events booked on the second floor in November.
desc: Reconcile two statements to find what both allow.
hint: Look for the weakest claim — the one that needs the least beyond the memos.
situation: Memo A (Facilities): 'All meeting rooms on the second floor are booked for training every Thursday in November.' Memo B (Training): 'Thursday training sessions in November are held in the second-floor meeting rooms, and all staff must attend at least one session.' Which must be true?
title: Paragraph inference: two memos
why: Memo B says all staff must attend at least one Thursday session held in second-floor rooms, so at least some staff will be in those rooms on some Thursday — choice 2. Choice 0 overreaches: training occupies the rooms, but 'no staff meetings can occur' assumes no room-sharing and ignores that training itself is a staff gathering. Choice 1 misreads 'at least one session' as 'every Thursday.' Choice 3 claims exclusivity ('only events') that neither memo states.

choices: assumes that because one event followed another, the first caused the second
attacks the character of the people who chose the paint
draws a conclusion about all clients from a single complaint
uses a word with two different meanings
desc: Name the error in a causal claim.
hint: What evidence links the paint to the complaints? Only timing.
situation: 'Ever since we repainted the lobby last spring, client complaints have dropped by half. The new paint color is clearly responsible for happier clients.' The argument's flaw is that it:
title: Logical flaw: post hoc reasoning
why: The only evidence is sequence (repaint, then fewer complaints) — the classic post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy: after it, therefore because of it. No rival causes were ruled out (staffing changes, seasonal patterns, etc.). The other choices describe ad hominem, hasty generalization, and equivocation — none of which occur here.

choices: relies on data from an unreliable source
presents only two options when others may exist
confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one
appeals to the popularity of overtime work
desc: Spot when an argument hides the middle options.
hint: Ask: are 'approve everything' and 'total failure' really the only two futures?
situation: 'We must either approve the full overtime budget or accept that the project will fail. Since failure is unacceptable, the overtime budget must be approved.' The argument is most vulnerable to criticism because it:
title: Logical flaw: false dilemma
why: This is a false dilemma: it frames the choice as approve-the-full-budget or project-failure, ignoring middle paths (partial budget, re-scoping, reassigning staff, extending the deadline). The argument collapses once a third option is admitted. The other flaws — bad source, necessary/sufficient confusion, popularity appeal — don't match the argument's structure.
